definition: Cheerfully hopeful, especially when things look difficult.
examples: Despite the weak sales figures, the founder remained sanguine about the company's future.
Economists are less sanguine than the minister about a quick recovery.

definition: Involving or eager for a great deal of bloodshed.
examples: The sanguinary battle left thousands dead on both sides.
Historians remember him as a sanguinary ruler who executed his rivals.

definition: Willing to act dishonestly in return for money; open to bribery.
examples: The venal official approved the permit only after receiving a payment.
Voters grew tired of a venal administration that sold favours to the highest bidder.

definition: Describing a fault that is minor and easily forgiven.
examples: Arriving five minutes late was a venial offence that nobody mentioned.
She treated his forgetfulness as a venial fault rather than a betrayal.

definition: To criticise or scold someone severely.
examples: The coach castigated the team for its careless defending.
Newspapers castigated the government over its slow response to the floods.

definition: To condemn someone or something in extremely harsh terms.
examples: The reviewer excoriated the film as lazy and dishonest.
In her speech she excoriated the bank for misleading its customers.

definition: To tell someone off sharply for something they have done wrong.
examples: The teacher upbraided the students for copying each other's work.
He upbraided himself for missing such an obvious error.

definition: Using very few words to say something.
examples: His laconic reply, a single 'no', ended the discussion.
The report was laconic, covering a year of work in two paragraphs.

definition: Quiet by nature and reluctant to talk.
examples: The taciturn farmer answered most questions with a nod.
She was taciturn at meetings but wrote long, thoughtful emails afterwards.

definition: Fond of talking and inclined to talk a lot.
examples: The loquacious taxi driver told us his life story before we reached the airport.
Normally loquacious, he fell silent when the results were announced.

definition: Talking too much, especially about unimportant things.
examples: A garrulous neighbour kept her at the gate for half an hour.
The lecture was spoiled by a garrulous host who rambled through every introduction.

definition: Lasting for only a very short time.
examples: Fame on social media is ephemeral; last month's star is forgotten today.
The desert flowers are ephemeral, blooming for a few days after rain.

definition: Passing quickly or staying only briefly; not permanent.
examples: The drug's side effects were mild and transient.
The town has a transient population of seasonal workers.

definition: Spending money or resources freely and wastefully.
examples: His prodigal spending emptied the inheritance within two years.
The city was prodigal with water until the reservoirs ran low.

definition: Remarkably great in size, amount or ability.
examples: She has a prodigious memory and can recite whole chapters.
Building the dam required a prodigious amount of concrete.

definition: Clever, original and inventive.
examples: The engineers found an ingenious way to cool the building without electricity.
It was an ingenious plan that used the rival's own rules against them.

definition: Innocent, trusting and openly honest, often to the point of being naive.
examples: His ingenuous questions revealed that he had never dealt with lawyers before.
She gave an ingenuous smile, unaware that she was being tricked.

definition: Not influenced by personal advantage; impartial.
examples: A dispute like this needs a disinterested judge with no stake in the outcome.
Her advice was disinterested, since she gained nothing whichever option we chose.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; deliberately unclear.
examples: The minister gave an equivocal answer that satisfied neither side.
Results from the first trial were equivocal, so a second study was planned.

definition: To speak vaguely in order to avoid committing to a position or telling the truth.
examples: Asked directly about the layoffs, the manager equivocated.
Stop equivocating and tell us whether you support the proposal.

definition: Having mixed or opposing feelings about something.
examples: She felt ambivalent about the promotion, which paid more but meant moving away.
Voters remain ambivalent about the reform, liking its aims but doubting its cost.

definition: To make something bad less severe or less harmful.
examples: Planting trees along the river helped mitigate the flooding.
The apology did little to mitigate the damage to his reputation.

definition: To make a bad situation better.
examples: New housing was built to ameliorate conditions in the crowded district.
The medicine ameliorated her symptoms but did not cure the disease.

definition: To make a problem or bad situation worse.
examples: Cutting the bus service will only exacerbate traffic in the city centre.
Stress exacerbated his headaches.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or soften one's attitude.
examples: The landlord remained obdurate and would not lower the rent.
Even faced with clear evidence, the obdurate witness stuck to his story.

definition: Unwilling to compromise or to change a position.
examples: Talks collapsed because both parties were intransigent on wages.
The intransigent committee rejected every amendment.

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and practically rather than by theory or ideals.
examples: She took a pragmatic approach and fixed the cheapest problems first.
A pragmatic leader, he worked with anyone who could get results.

definition: Insisting that one's beliefs are certainly true and refusing to consider other views.
examples: He was so dogmatic about his diet that he lectured everyone at dinner.
Science advances when researchers are curious rather than dogmatic.

definition: To drain someone of energy or strength.
examples: The heat and humidity enervated the hikers by midday.
Months of night shifts had enervated her completely.

definition: To give energy, strength or new life to someone or something.
examples: A swim in the cold lake invigorated him.
The new director invigorated a department that had drifted for years.

definition: To praise someone or something highly, especially in public.
examples: Critics lauded the novel for its honesty.
The mayor lauded the volunteers who had rebuilt the school.

definition: To praise something enthusiastically.
examples: The brochure extols the benefits of mountain air.
He extolled his mentor's patience in every interview.

definition: To speak about someone or something as being of little worth.
examples: He disparaged his rival's research as mere guesswork.
It is easy to disparage popular music, but writing a good song is hard.

definition: To unfairly attack the reputation or value of someone or something.
examples: The campaign tried to denigrate the candidate by spreading rumours.
She refused to denigrate her former colleagues, whatever she thought of them.

definition: Having or showing deep knowledge gained from study.
examples: The erudite professor quoted from memory in four languages.
Her erudite essay traced the idea back to ancient Greece.

definition: Too concerned with small details or formal rules, especially in showing off learning.
examples: His pedantic corrections of every comma annoyed the whole team.
It may sound pedantic, but the two terms do not mean the same thing.

definition: Understood by or meant for only a small group with special knowledge.
examples: The lecture was full of esoteric references that only specialists followed.
He collects esoteric facts about medieval coinage.

definition: Known or understood by very few people; mysterious.
examples: The tax code is full of arcane rules that confuse even accountants.
She learned the arcane rituals of the old guild.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is complex or highly abstract.
examples: The philosopher's abstruse arguments lost most of the audience.
He has a gift for explaining abstruse mathematics in plain language.

definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand.
examples: Her lucid explanation made the theory seem simple.
The guide is short, lucid and free of jargon.

definition: To make something unclear or hard to understand, often on purpose.
examples: The company used technical jargon to obfuscate the real cost.
Long footnotes obfuscated what should have been a simple point.

definition: Changing mood or behaviour suddenly and without good reason.
examples: The capricious manager praised a plan on Monday and cancelled it on Tuesday.
Mountain weather is capricious, so carry a jacket even on a sunny day.

definition: Having moods or opinions that change quickly and unpredictably.
examples: The mercurial striker could win a match or be sent off in the first ten minutes.
Working for such a mercurial boss kept everyone on edge.

definition: Very attentive to detail and hard to please, especially about cleanliness or accuracy.
examples: He is fastidious about his desk, with every pen in its place.
A fastidious editor, she checked each date against the original source.

definition: Extremely careful and precise about every detail.
examples: The detective kept meticulous notes on every interview.
Restoring the painting took two years of meticulous work.

definition: Ordinary and unimaginative; lacking anything poetic or exciting.
examples: The mystery had a prosaic explanation: a faulty switch.
After the adventure, his prosaic office job felt dull.

definition: So ordinary and unoriginal that it is boring.
examples: The speech was a string of banal remarks about teamwork.
What began as a fresh idea became banal through endless repetition.

definition: Something that differs from what is normal or expected.
examples: A snowstorm in May is an anomaly in this region.
The auditors flagged several anomalies in the accounts.

definition: A very small amount of something; a shortage.
examples: The study was limited by a paucity of reliable data.
There is a paucity of affordable housing near the campus.

definition: A very large amount of something, often more than is needed.
examples: Shoppers face a plethora of nearly identical phone plans.
The festival offered a plethora of workshops, far more than anyone could attend.
